entries.title: a foreign call does not resize an array
entries.body:
A `declare function` now has `resizesArray = false`. C is lent a `u8[]`'s
`buf->data` and a `string`'s `s->data` for the call. It never gets an array
header, so it can write bytes but cannot move a `len` or a `data` pointer
(docs/wp40-ffi-buffers-handles.md §3c). It cannot re-enter Nish to do it
either: an exported function that C calls back reaches no array its caller
holds, because a module has no `let`, no array `const` and no `static` field.
Every other worst-case fact a foreign callee carries stays: `willReturn`,
`sharedWrite`, `writesPastParams`, `writesElsewhere` and `readsMemory`. The
checker's index proof does not read the fact, so `bounds.ts` and `ranges.ts`
still forget every length at a foreign call (Q15), and the NL9007 on
`buf[i]` after a `read` stays.

Three emitter effects move, and the user functions that resize keep them all.
The IR below is `tests/cases/ffi_buffer_no_resize` compiled by 0.19.0
(before) and by this change (after).

- **A compound store after the call** (`addCount`,
  `buf[i] += toU8(read(fd, buf, toU64(buf.length)))`). The store no longer
  reloads `len`, re-checks and re-addresses the element after the call. It
  stores to the slot `%16` it proved before the call:

      before:
        %28 = add i8 %17, %27
        %29 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %11, i64 0, i32 0
        %30 = load i64, i64* %29, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !10
        %31 = icmp ult i64 %12, %30
        br i1 %31, label %bounds.ok, label %bounds.fail
      bounds.fail:
        call void @nish_panic_index(i64 %12, i64 %30)
        unreachable
      bounds.ok:
        %32 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %11, i64 0, i32 2
        %33 = load i8*, i8** %32, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !11
        %34 = bitcast i8* %33 to i8*
        %35 = getelementptr inbounds i8, i8* %34, i64 %12
        store i8 %28, i8* %35, align 1, !alias.scope !4, !noalias !3, !tbaa !13
      after:
        %28 = add i8 %17, %27
        store i8 %28, i8* %16, align 1, !alias.scope !4, !noalias !3, !tbaa !13

- **The `len` and `data` hoist in a counted loop** (`sumCounted`,
  `for (let i = 0; i < buf.length; i++) { read(fd, buf, 1); s += toI32(buf[i]) }`).
  The preheader loads them once. Before, the loop condition and the bounds
  check each reloaded `len` per iteration, and the element access reloaded
  `data`:

      preheader (after only):
        %4 = load %struct.nish_array*, %struct.nish_array** %buf.addr, align 8
        %5 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %4, i64 0, i32 0
        %6 = load i64, i64* %5, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !10
        %7 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %4, i64 0, i32 2
        %8 = load i8*, i8** %7, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !11
      for.cond, before:
        %5 = load %struct.nish_array*, %struct.nish_array** %buf.addr, align 8
        %6 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %5, i64 0, i32 0
        %7 = load i64, i64* %6, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !10
        %8 = trunc i64 %7 to i32
      for.cond, after:
        %10 = trunc i64 %6 to i32
      the check after `read`, before:
        %21 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %18, i64 0, i32 0
        %22 = load i64, i64* %21, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !10
        %23 = icmp ult i64 %20, %22
        ...
        %24 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %18, i64 0, i32 2
        %25 = load i8*, i8** %24, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !11
      the check after `read`, after:
        %22 = icmp ult i64 %21, %6
        ...
        %23 = bitcast i8* %8 to i8*

- **A `for…of` whose body calls C counts as bounded** (`sumEach`,
  `for (const b of buf) { read(fd, buf, 1); s += toI32(b) }`). Its `.ll` does
  not move, because `read`'s `willReturn = false` still keeps `willreturn` off
  the caller. The fact shows in the `--emit-checked` facts line:

      before: facts: effect=write willReturn=false hasLoops=true loopsBounded=false readsMemory=true ...
      after:  facts: effect=write willReturn=false hasLoops=true loopsBounded=true readsMemory=true ...

  The same line moves for `findOf` (strdup) and `ofs` (strerror) in their
  `tests/self/goldens/checked/` dumps.

B1.2's narrow proof (`foreignBufferCountProven`) reads the fact too, through
`bodyMayExtend`, so it widens. A later argument that is itself a foreign call
now proves `toU64(buf.length)` and drops the `ffi-length` check. A later
argument that is a user function calling C *and* popping keeps it. Both are
pinned in `tests/cases/panics_ffi_length_foreign_arg`. For `credited`,
`pwrite(-1, buf, toU64(buf.length), lseek(-1, 0, 1))`:

      before:
        %15 = call i64 @lseek(i32 -1, i64 0, i32 1)
        %16 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %9, i64 0, i32 0
        %17 = load i64, i64* %16, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !10
        %18 = icmp ule i64 %14, %17
        br i1 %18, label %ffi.ok, label %ffi.length
      ffi.length:
        call void @nish_panic(i8* bitcast ({ i64, [71 x i8] }* @.str.0 to i8*))
        unreachable
      ffi.ok:
        %19 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %9, i64 0, i32 2
        %20 = load i8*, i8** %19, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !11
        %21 = call i64 @pwrite(i32 -1, i8* %20, i64 %14, i64 %15)
      after:
        %15 = call i64 @lseek(i32 -1, i64 0, i32 1)
        %16 = getelementptr inbounds %struct.nish_array, %struct.nish_array* %9, i64 0, i32 2
        %17 = load i8*, i8** %16, align 8, !alias.scope !3, !noalias !4, !tbaa !11
        %18 = call i64 @pwrite(i32 -1, i8* %17, i64 %14, i64 %15)

`--emit-panics` lists that site as `proven: true` (it was `false`). In
`uncredited`, the later argument is `rewound(buf)`, which calls `lseek` and
then pops. The site stays `proven: false`, the IR keeps `ffi.length`, and the
native run compares 4 against 3 and panics with "`pwrite`: argument 3 (n)
counts more bytes than argument 2 (buf) holds". No other golden moved.

The pins in `tests/cases/ffi_buffer_no_resize` are `drain`, a user function
that reads and then pops. It is called from each of the three shapes, along
with a constructor that calls C, reached by `new`. A stale hoist in those
pins would show twice. In the golden, each drain function would lose its
per-iteration reload, its re-check or `loopsBounded=false`. In the round trip,
`sumDrained` would iterate past the length `drain` shrank and print another
sum, or panic.

Measured: no change outside the noise band on a counted loop that calls
`read` 2,048,000 times from /dev/zero, a loop bound by the syscall. Over 7
interleaved rounds the medians were 337 ms before and 340 ms after, against
337 / 352 ms for the before binary timed against a byte-identical copy of
itself.

entries.title: seed the interop image from a published release
entries.body:
Interop's server image pinned its seed to package.json's version, which names a release with no SHA256SUMS from the moment the Release PR merges until release.yml publishes it. Every Interop run in that window, starting with the release commit's own push, failed to fetch its seed.

The image now seeds from the newest published release, as ci.yml does, or from a SEED_VERSION build argument. interop.yml is also a reusable workflow with a `seed` input, and release.yml gains an `interop` job that needs `release` and runs it with the tag it just published, beside `npm`.

entries.title: tell an integer-valued JSON number by its value
entries.body:
`JsonTokenizer.isIntegral()` and `JsonDocument.isIntegral(v)` answer whether a
JSON number's value is a whole number, however it is written: `1.0`, `1e2`,
`100e-2`, `12345678901234567890.0` and `1e400` are; `1.5`, `10e-2` and
`1e-400` are not. That is JSON Schema 2020-12's "integer", and the tokenizer
method answers it on the current token, so a validator can apply the rule
during the parse without building a document. The existing readers keep the
spelling rule: `isInteger`, `isI64`, `isU64` and the `integral` field still
say no to `1.0`.

The answer comes from the token's text, never a double. With F fraction
digits, z trailing zeros and exponent E, a number whose digits are not all
zero is whole when E >= F - z. The exponent's digits are compared with that
one bound and never summed past it or past an i32, so an exponent of any
length is exact and cannot overflow, with the same answer under Node and
natively. docs/security/json.md records the bound.

entries.title: split runtime-net three ways and run only the platform's checks on macOS
entries.body:
* ci: split runtime-net three ways and deal crypto-bench across the test shards

The macOS `runtime-net` job ran its 188 `net_` link programs one at a time,
and a mac runner took from 11 to over 28 minutes for them on one image; run
39877823045's first attempt was cancelled by the job's 30-minute limit a few
programs from the end. It now runs as three shards (`node tests/run.js net_
--shard <i>/3`), each with a 20-minute limit. A filtered run deals only the
link programs its filter selects and starts shard 1 at nothing; dealt from
the whole table, the `net_` programs fell 1.3, 4.2, 7.4 and 7.6 minutes to four
shards rather than about 5 each.

Shard 1 of the `test` job took 17 to 19 minutes against about 8 for the
others, because crypto-bench (4.5 minutes, building every twin of five
families) ran in its shard-1-only tail. crypto-bench is now dealt like WP14
self-hosting: both are listed in `DEALT_SECTIONS`, sit before the point where
other shards stop, and carry their cost in tests/shard-costs.json, which is
regenerated from run 39878648000's four shards.

Each link program's per-module `llvm-as` and `opt -passes=verify` now run
`defaultJobs()` at a time, and its `--emit-panics` compile runs beside them;
the checks are still made in module order, with the same output. Delegations
now name "shard i/n of this job", since two jobs are sharded.

Measured: `node tests/run.js net_relay_bad` (15 link programs), 3m07s -> 2m21s on a 4-core container, one run each, identical PASS lines
Tests: node tests/run.js net_relay_bad --shard 1/3, 2/3, 3/3 (union equals the unsharded run's checks)

* ci: run only the platform's checks of each net_ program on macOS

`node tests/run.js --delegate-ir-checks`, which the `runtime-net` job now
passes, links and runs each tests/link program and leaves every check of its
compile to the Linux `test` job: the module goldens, llvm-as and opt, the

and the flag is honoured only under GitHub Actions, so a local run still makes
every check. A check reads ci.yml and fails if another job asks for the
delegation or the `test` job's suite line takes a filter.

entries.title: tie NL8001's loop cursor to the string it counts
entries.body:
A loop bounded by a UTF-8 offset now takes a local as its cursor only
when the loop hands it to a method of the string the offset counted.
Before, any string's method made the cursor, so a loop over
`word.length` that read only `other.charCodeAt(i)` was quiet; it is now
reported. Once the offset has crossed into another function the string
it counted is out of reach, and any string's method still makes the
cursor there.

The arms that treated a string index as a cursor or a byte read are
gone: only an array can be indexed, so the index picks an element. An
offset leaving a parallel arrow is reported only for the map forms,
which store each answer in an array; a `spawn` thunk answers `void`.
The walk-limits fixture now shows each documented gap: the return
chain past the hop limit, a recursive helper, a parallel relay, a
spawned answer and a crossed-function cursor.

Fixes #829

entries.title: split the Node runtime into a host-agnostic core and a Node adapter
entries.body:
runtime/shim.mjs mixed what a program computes with what it asks of
Node. Every host-agnostic export now lives in runtime/core/*.mjs behind
runtime/core.mjs, which names no node: module, process or Buffer, and
every host-bound call goes through one installed host object in
runtime/core/host.mjs; until a host is installed each member throws
NishNoHost naming what was asked for. runtime/node.mjs holds the Node
bodies unchanged and installs them on import, and shim.mjs is now that
adapter plus the core, exporting every name it had, so every prelude,
differential and frozen-rewrite check passes unmodified. This is
wp33's R3 first half; the browser adapter and the package entry points
follow.

entries.title: add nish/term, terminal frames and key decoding with no I/O
entries.body:
`std/term` (imported as "nish/term") is the drawing half of a terminal UI.
It turns state into strings and bytes into events and does no I/O itself:
it reaches no capability, its output is golden-tested, and it prints the
same bytes under Node as natively.

- `Screen` is width × height cells (code point, foreground, background,
  bold/inverse), double-buffered. `flush()` returns the least ANSI that turns
  the last frame into this one: a cursor move only where a run starts, only
  the changed runs, a short gap bridged rather than jumped, and one SGR per
  change of style. The byte buffer is sized by `resize`, so a frame loop
  takes back each pass's string. With `sync` set, each flush that changes
  anything is wrapped in the synchronized-output escapes (DEC mode 2026),
  which kitty, foot, WezTerm and iTerm2 honour, so a frame drawn at 120 or
  240 Hz is never shown half painted. A cell is printed only when it holds a
  printable scalar: a C0 or C1 control, DEL, a surrogate or a negative goes
  as U+FFFD, so untrusted text in a cell cannot open an escape.
- `Canvas` draws pixels on a Screen with the upper half block "▀"
  (foreground = top pixel, background = bottom pixel), with `setPixel`,
  `fillRect`, `line` and text over the pixels.
- Colours are 24-bit `rgb`. A flag the caller passes switches to the nearest
  of the 256-colour palette (`paletteIndex`), so reading COLORTERM stays
  outside the module.
- The escapes are functions: alternate screen enter/leave, cursor hide/show,
  clear, reset, move, and `beginSync`/`endSync`.
- `KeyDecoder` turns bytes into key events: arrows as ESC [ A–D and
  ESC O A–D, Enter, Space, Tab, Backspace, Escape, Ctrl-C (byte 3) and
  printable UTF-8. It holds a partial sequence across calls and decides a
  lone ESC by a timeout the caller supplies to `feed` and `poll`. Invalid
  UTF-8 and C1 controls decode to U+FFFD.
- `FixedStep(stepsPerSecond, maxSteps)` is a fixed-step clock on the
  caller's time: `advance(nowMs)` answers the whole steps since the last
  call, `alpha()` the remainder for drawing in between, and a clock more
  than `maxSteps` behind drops the backlog and keeps its phase.

Terminal size, raw mode and stdin are left to builtins; width and height
are parameters.
metrics: flush of a full 200x60 frame change (one colour) 72-113 us, median ~85 us; whole frame 101-160 us (3 runs x 5 rounds)
flush of a one-cell change on 200x60 23-31 us
canvas game frame on 200x60 (clear, 40 bricks, paddle, ball) 101-175 us whole, flush 24-36 us
worst case, a different 24-bit fg and bg in every cell (~380 KB out), flush 500-750 us, under 1 ms

entries.title: publish nish/runtime with a browser adapter and declarations
entries.body:
The package now has three entry points for a JavaScript or TypeScript
caller: nish/runtime, the host-agnostic core; nish/runtime/node; and
nish/runtime/browser, a new adapter built from web globals alone. The
browser host prints line-buffered to the console, throws a NishExit
carrying the 8-bit exit code, reads the monotonic clock from
performance.now, answers getenv with null, and panics naming the
browser on every file-system or process call. runtime/core.d.ts and
runtime/core/*.d.ts declare every helper, with i64 and u64 as bigint and
every other width as number. A test loads the core and the browser
adapter in a vm context holding only web globals and runs them, and the
new guide page, "Back to TypeScript", covers the entry points, what each
host answers, and that Bun is untested.

entries.title: check the owned foreign handle class
entries.body:
A class with a `CPtr` or `CPtr | null` field is a handle class: it owns the C
resource, its constructor writes the field once from a `declare function`, its
methods read it only as `this.f`, and its `[Symbol.dispose]` is exactly the
close, declared once with no modifier. A handle is opened by `using`, called,
or lent to a parameter of its type, and refused everywhere else. `using` of a
handle class is refused (NL2573, "not lowered yet") until a later release emits
the close at every exit of its block, so the checker never accepts a handle that
nothing closes. A generic class's type arguments are now checked where it is
instantiated, as a generic function's were, so `new Empty<CPtr>()` is refused.

entries.title: nish/yaml, a YAML parser with byte ranges, lines and paths
entries.body:
nish/yaml parses a YAML 1.2 stream into a YamlStream: struct-of-arrays
storage with i32 handles, a [start, end) byte range on every node, pair and
diagnostic, and scalars decoded and resolved to the core schema only when
read. It never panics on its input; problems come back as diagnostics with
the codes and spellings @amritk/yaml uses. nish/yaml-lines turns an offset
into a 1-based line, a character column and a byte column, so a linter can
print `line:col CODE message`. Paths resolve to a node or to the pair whose
key a report should point at, the last duplicate key winning.

entries.title: write a program back out as TypeScript with --emit-ts
entries.body:
`nish <entry> --emit-ts <dir>` writes the checked program back out as
TypeScript that Node runs with type stripping. Each root-package module is
written at its path relative to the directory the root modules share, and
each standard-library module the program reaches is written under nish/.
Every other nish: builtin import becomes nish/runtime, and entry.ts
installs the Node host, calls main and exits with its answer. A module
with no class-C site is copied byte for byte, and type imports are marked
so strip-types drops them.

A module that declares C functions is refused with NL4010, and signals or
nish:net, imported or used as globals, with NL4011. Either refusal writes
no file. A missing or empty directory, a clashing output flag, an
unwritable layout, or an output path that would land on one of the
program's own modules exits 2 before anything is written. The runtime
import goes after the leading comments and any #! line, where the lexer
says they end, so it never splits a line.

The per-construct translations are stubs here; later stages fill them in.
tests/differential/emit-ts.js runs the whole corpus natively and through
--emit-ts under Node, comparing stdout, stderr and exit status. It fails
on an unlisted disagreement, on a listed program that starts agreeing,
moves row or disappears, and on any emit, build or native-timeout error.
The programs the stubs cannot yet translate are listed by row in the
generated tests/differential/emit-ts-known.txt.

entries.title: compare nish/yaml with @amritk/yaml
entries.body:
bench/yaml-compare/ times nish/yaml against @amritk/yaml 0.8.0 under Node (and Bun when installed) on five pinned fixtures: an OpenAPI description, a multi-document Kubernetes manifest, a JSON-as-YAML file, a CI workflow full of block scalars, and a compose file with anchors and merge keys. Two workloads: parse, and parse plus a walk that reads every scalar's text. Both sides print a checksum of document count, node count per kind and error count, and a run whose checksums disagree fails. tests/run.js holds the Nish runner to a committed sample without the network; the bench itself never runs in npm test.

The baseline, on the parser before any tuning, has nish/yaml ahead in every row, 1.11x to 2.57x of @amritk/yaml under Node.
metrics: Node/Nish median 1.11x (airflow walk) to 2.57x (citm parse), noise band 0.0-2.5%

entries.title: add nish/regex, a linear-time regex engine with a lazy DFA
entries.body:
`nish/regex` matches regular expressions with JavaScript `RegExp` semantics
(leftmost-first alternation, JS captures) in time linear in the text and in
bounded memory, with no backtracking. A Pike VM gives captures and is the
fallback. A lazy DFA, capped at 2,048 states and 1 MiB of transitions, does
the search, and a reverse DFA finds the leftmost start. Prefilters skip to
candidates: `indexOf` for a literal prefix, a first-byte table, an
inner-literal search, and the new runtime kernel `nish_regex_scan`, which
tests sixteen or thirty-two starts at a time against per-position byte sets.

The API is `regexCompile(pattern, flags)` returning a `Result`, then `test`,
`exec`, `find`, `count`, `replace` (with `$1` and `$<name>`) and `split`,
plus `regexEscape`. Against Rust's `regex` crate on nine patterns it is
faster on six and within 12% on digits, within 22% on captures.

entries.title: add issue forms that ask for what a fix needs
entries.body:
* docs: add issue forms that ask for what a fix needs

Bug reports, language or library requests and documentation problems now
open as GitHub issue forms. The bug form requires what a fix starts from:
the version or commit, install route, platform, the smallest program that
compiles as pasted, the exact command line, the full output and exit
code, and the expected behaviour with the rule or Node output behind it.
It also asks for the last good version, so a fix can begin from a bisect.
Blank issues are off. The chooser links private vulnerability reporting,
the FAQ and the known inconsistencies.

The README, FAQ, INSTALL and the CLI guide page told a reporter that
`NISH_DEBUG=1` prints a stack trace for exit 70. The self-hosted compiler
has none, and says so, so they now ask for the input, the command line
and the printed report.

* build: exempt .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE from the kebab-case file-name rule

GitHub reads issue forms only from a directory spelled that way, so it joins node_modules as a name a tool looks for.

entries.title: cache interop's tshark packages and retry them off the Azure mirror
entries.body: The quic-interop-runner jobs install tshark, 26.5 MB of packages, most of it libwireshark17t64. The Azure Ubuntu mirror sometimes serves that at a trickle that never trips apt's idle timeout, so the step's five-minute limit fired before any case ran. As in ci.yml's test job, the .debs are now kept in the Actions cache keyed by runner image, and on a miss each download attempt is cut at a minute and retried without the Azure mirror.

entries.title: count code points in std/text
entries.body: codePointLength(text) returns the number of Unicode code points in a string, the count JSON Schema's minLength and maxLength use, where .length counts UTF-8 bytes natively and UTF-16 units under Node. It reads which units the host gives and walks them accordingly: natively it counts non-continuation bytes, with the host probe folded away under -O2 and the walk vectorized; under Node it counts UTF-16 units less each paired low surrogate. The two hosts agree on any string written in the source, and differ only on text built from bytes and on text that is not well-formed, both documented and pinned by tests.

entries.title: nish/yaml paths follow merge keys, held to the yaml-test-suite
entries.body:
* feat(std): nish/yaml paths follow merge keys, held to the yaml-test-suite

pathNode and pathPair now look a key a map does not hold up in the maps
its << merge keys name, in order: the map's own keys win, then the first
merged map listed, depth first, with a visited check and the 100-hop
bound so a recursive alias ends. With merge off, << is an ordinary key.

A new link test runs the yaml-test-suite: error cases must report an
error, valid ones none, and each document must equal the case's JSON.
A plain scalar's continuation line of blanks, tabs included, is now an
empty line.

* feat(std): nish/yaml reports a merge key that names no map, and an empty block scalar ends at its header

A << value that is not a map, an alias to one or a sequence of those is
a BAD_MERGE error, on the value, on each bad item of a sequence, or on
the key when the value is empty. An empty block scalar's range now ends
at its header instead of the start of the next line. The guide shows a
path through a merge key.

* style(std): format nish/yaml

* fix(std): type the merge search's start depth for f64 number mode

A `<<` key tagged `!!merge` is a merge key like an untagged one, and any
other tag makes it an ordinary key. A merge value may now be an alias to a
sequence of maps, which paths already followed; an item that is not a map
is reported on the alias. The path walker reuses one array to track the
maps a merge search has visited, rather than allocating one per step.

A path step that searched merge keys checked every map it had been through
in a list, so one step over a map with N merge sources cost about N^2/2
compares: 50k sources written as `<<: [{}, {}, ...]` stalled a single
pathNode call for a second. Each node of the stream now carries the stamp
of the last step that searched it, and a step takes a new stamp instead of

A plain scalar's line of only spaces and tabs is an empty line, so it folds

entries.title: group and colour --help, and keep it plain for agents
entries.body:
nish --help is grouped by purpose (Build, Check, Capabilities, Interop,
Inspect, Code generation), followed by the exit codes and examples. It is
coloured on a terminal and plain when piped, under NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb.

Under a coding agent (CLAUDECODE, GEMINI_CLI or NISH_AGENT=1) the help is
always plain and ends with an Agents section naming the installed
docs/AI.md by absolute path, plus --json, --fix and nish run. docs/AI.md
now ships in the platform package and the release tarball so that path
exists after an npm install. An unknown flag prints a one-line hint to
nish --help instead of the whole menu, and still exits 2.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: translate the string rows in --emit-ts
entries.body:
Nish counts string offsets in UTF-8 bytes and Node counts them in UTF-16
units, so `--emit-ts` now writes every string member that reads or gives
an offset as a call of the core helper that counts bytes: `.length`,
`charCodeAt`, `indexOf`, `slice` and `substring` on a string, and a
string's `.length` closing a `?.` chain as `strLenOpt`. `String.fromBytes`
decodes its range as UTF-8, and `String.fromCharCode` and `Number` of a
string go through the core's helpers rather than the globals.

The row names what it still leaves apart: byte-offset methods inside a
`?.` chain (right for ASCII only), `fromCharCode` at 128 and above
(Latin-1, as the C row), the lossy U+FFFD decode, and helper names that
may clash with a program's own bindings. The core strings module caches
the last string's UTF-8 bytes and searches them with
`Uint8Array.indexOf`, so repeated offset calls on one string stop
re-encoding it.

Measured: indexOf x200 on a 24 KB string 18 ms -> 1.7 ms; charCodeAt over
every byte 620 ms -> 0.5 ms; adversarial indexOf 23 ms -> 27 ms (Node 22,
single runs)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: add nish:term, terminal input for real-time terminal programs
entries.body:
A Nish program can now read keys as they are pressed. `nish:term` adds five
builtins, each also a global: `readStdin(buf, off, len)` reads what is waiting
on stdin without blocking (-11 when nothing is), `waitStdin(timeoutMs)` waits
until stdin is readable and serves as a frame clock, `isTerminal(fd)`,
`terminalSize()` and `setRawMode(on)`. They need the new `tty` capability, not
`net`, and pair with the std `nish/term` module for drawing.

stdin is never made non-blocking, since that flag is shared with the shell;
`readStdin` asks `select` first instead. Raw mode keeps `ISIG` and `OPOST`, so
Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z and "\n" behave as before. The saved terminal comes back on
`setRawMode(false)`, at exit, on every panic, and on each signal whose default
ends the program, faults included, through handlers on an alternate stack.
Ctrl-Z restores the terminal while the program is stopped and `fg` puts raw
mode back, and a wait a stop interrupts still ends at its deadline. The C
runtime gains a ninth translation unit, linked only by programs that call
these. Under WASI the reads wait and the terminal questions answer "not a
terminal"; under Node `isTerminal` and `terminalSize` answer and the others
throw.
metrics: runtime-term.c .text is 1,419 bytes under a 1,536-byte ceiling (clang 18 -Oz, deterministic)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: translate the number rows in --emit-ts
entries.body:
A program translated with `--emit-ts` now prints under Node what its native
build prints for the number rows. An i32 `+ - *` that may overflow panics
through `checkedAdd`, `checkedSub` and `checkedMul`; a proven or
`--wrapping` one wraps with `| 0` and `Math.imul`. Integer `/` and `%` go
through `idiv` and `irem`, which panic on zero and on MIN / -1. u8, u16 and
u32 wrap with masks and `>>> 0`, i64 and u64 are `bigint`, `>>>` on i32
keeps its sign width, the saturating conversions go through `convert`, f32
arithmetic rounds with `Math.fround`, and `Math.min`, `max` and `round` keep
native NaN and -0 answers. An i64 or u64 offset passed to `fill` or to a
string method becomes a number before the call, so the strings row still
counts UTF-8 bytes.

A compound assignment whose target holds a call, a step or an element read
cannot be written as `x = x op e` without reading that target twice, so it
is refused with NL4012 rather than emitted wrong. The Node host now makes
stdout and stderr blocking, so a program's output is never cut short when
it exits under load.

Measured: 55 of 64 parallel runs of corpus/bit_fnv1a truncated before the
blocking-stdout change, 0 of 256 after
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: translate orReturn, Result and enums in --emit-ts
entries.body:
`--emit-ts` now translates the control row. A `Result`'s `orReturn` whose
statement can take a prelude becomes a temporary, an `isErr` test and a
return of the `Err`, hoisted before the statement in the order the calls
run. Anywhere a hoist could change what runs or in what order — the right
of `&&`, `||` or `??`, a `?:` branch, past a `?.`, after an effect, a field
or element read, a write the call makes to a local read earlier, or an
operand that may panic — the call stays and its function is wrapped so the
runtime's thrown propagation comes back as the `Err`. An enum becomes a
`const` object with the checker's member values and a type of its values,
`Result` annotations import the runtime's `Result`, and `Arena` members
become the runtime's arena functions.

The composer gains a prelude contract (`canHoist`, `hoist`, `temporary`)
that writes each block statement's preludes before it, with temporaries
numbered once per module so every generic instance writes the same text.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: `using` of a handle class closes it at every exit of its block
entries.body:
A `using f = new File(p)` of a WP40 handle class now lowers: every exit
of its block -- fall-through, a non-tail return, break and continue,
scope joins and orReturn() -- calls the close its [Symbol.dispose] names
on the CPtr field once, exactly as the dispose spells it (a null test
only when the dispose has one, whatever the field's type). A panic or
process.exit does not close. Each declarator of a `using` opens before
the next initialiser runs (Q12(a)), so one that leaves the function
closes the ones before it. break, continue and fall-through close
last-opened-first; a return joins its scopes, computes its value, closes
handles and locks innermost first, then releases arenas. NL2573 is
retired.

entries.title: byte-class runs and copyBytes in nish/bytes, on runtime kernels
entries.body:
* perf(std): parse JSON floats with Eisel-Lemire in nish/json-tokenizer

`numberF64` read a number itself only when Clinger's exact path applied (at
most 15 significant digits, a decimal exponent within ±22) and handed every
other number to `parseFloat`. canada.json's coordinates have 16 and 17
digits, so each one went to `strtod`, more than half of canada's tokenize
time. Numbers of up to 19 significant digits now take Eisel-Lemire: one
64×64→128-bit product of the significand and a 128-bit power of five, or
two when the first is ambiguous, then rounding to even. Mushtak and Lemire
proved the product always decides the rounding for 19 digits or fewer, so
there is no fallback; only a longer significand still calls `parseFloat`.

The algorithm is ported from fast_float at 0de7a21 under BSL-1.0, with its
notice and a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md row. The table of 651 powers of five is
generated by scripts/gen-json-pow5.mjs with BigInt, and tests/run.js checks
the region in std/json-tokenizer.ts is byte for byte what it writes. The
code is ordinary Nish, so Node runs it too and is checked by the same tests.

Every answer is bit-for-bit parseFloat's on canada.json's 978,519 numbers,
on JSONTestSuite, and on 10^8 random doubles printed shortest and at 17
digits; new checks pin subnormals, the smallest normal, the largest finite
value, the first overflow, 19 and 20 digits and halfway cases.

Measured: canada tokenize 18.03 -> 6.50 ms (2.78x), citm 2.10 -> 1.80 ms (1.17x), twitter unchanged; min ns over interleaved rounds, bands at most 6.9%
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#6, docs/security/json.md
Tests: tests/link/std_json_tokenizer

* docs: record bench/json-compare after Eisel-Lemire in numberF64

canada.json now tokenizes in 6.29 ms at the minimum, 1.06x simdjson's
On-Demand; citm_catalog in 1.82 ms (1.59x) and twitter in 0.99 ms (2.20x).

Measured: noise bands 0.2% twitter, 2.0% citm, canada within 1%, on the minimums
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#6

* fix(std): compile numberF64's Eisel-Lemire under --number-mode f64

Under `--number-mode f64` a literal on the left of an operator, and a sum of
literals, is an `f64`, so three of jsonTokEiselLemire's i32 expressions did
not compile there and the performance gate refused nish/json-tokenizer,
nish/json-typed and nish/json-value. The typed operand now comes first, and
upstream's two constant sums are folded.

Tests: tests/run.js performance

* feat(std): byte-class runs and copyBytes in nish/bytes, on runtime kernels

nish/bytes gains skipBlank, skipDigits and skipJsonText, the first index in
a clamped range whose byte is not a JSON blank, a digit or a byte a JSON
string holds as itself (printable ASCII but `"` and `\`, and well-formed
UTF-8), and copyBytes, a window copied as one move that panics on a range
outside its array. Each body calls a private walker, which is what runs
under Node; natively the compiler replaces the call with a kernel of the
new runtime/runtime-bytes.c (scalar, SSE2/NEON/wasm SIMD and AVX2 paths,
pinned by NISH_SIMD), or llvm.memmove for the copy. The unit is 1,303
bytes of text against a 1,536 budget; folded into runtime-simd.c the two
would have measured 1,960 against its 768. A freestanding wasm32 build
links it when the IR names its symbols, as it does runtime-aes.c.

nish/json-tokenizer walks blanks and string bodies on these kernels after
an inline check of the first bytes, and copies a string's plain runs into
its decode buffer with copyBytes. Digits stay an inline loop: a number's
runs are shorter than a call is worth. The runs are variable-time, and
std/crypto does not call them.

Measured: tokenize twitter 1.48x, citm_catalog 1.23x to 1.31x, canada 0.93x against a3935f1, 9 interleaved rounds, noise band 3-5%
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#7-stages-and-the-bar-each-must-clear, docs/LANGUAGE.md#byte-runs-skipblank-skipdigits-skipjsontext-and-copybytes-in-nishbytes
Tests: tests/link/std_bytes_runs, tests/link/std_bytes_copy_outside, tests/simd/byte-runs.c

* docs: record S6a in wp38 and write the S6c structural-index design

S6a's section now says what was built: runtime-bytes.c as a unit of its own,
the text class with DEL and in-kernel UTF-8, the measured guards, copyBytes in
stringInto, and the writer's escape scan left as a follow-up. Q6 is decided as
nish/bytes. S6c's design (Q5) is written for the owner: one bitmap per 64-byte
block built in chunks into a fixed buffer, the kernel's bits as hints only, so
every error stays the scalar code's at its offset. Nothing of S6c is built.

Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#8-decisions

* docs: record bench/json-compare after the byte-class kernels

twitter.json now tokenizes in 0.74 ms at the minimum, 1.55x behind simdjson's
On-Demand (2.20x before), and citm_catalog in 1.47 ms, 1.24x behind (1.59x
before). canada.json is 6.96 ms, 1.10x behind. Against the 06645ecf record
S6a's bar is read from, tokenize is 1.69x faster on twitter and 1.63x on citm,
so the stage's 1.2x bar is met. The serialize part is not reached: the writer
was not changed.

Measured: noise bands 0.1% twitter, 6.6% citm, 2.3% canada on the minimums; every other implementation's minimum rose 5-7% against the previous record, a noisier host
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#7-stages-and-the-bar-each-must-clear

* fix(std): keep the tokenizer's digit loop provably in bounds

S6a folded the digit loop's two bounds into one clamped `to`, which the range
proof cannot follow, so the read kept its bounds check and the performance gate
failed for std/json-tokenizer.ts and its importers. The loop tests `end` and the
array's length again, as it did before S6a.

Tests: node tests/run.js performance

* test(cli): count runtime-bytes.c among the runtime units a link compiles

runtime-bytes.c made the runtime nine translation units, but the cpu-level test
still counted eight -march'd compiles, so it failed. The runtime-cache tests,
the CLI-11 record, the run cache's comments, INSTALL.md and the master plan now
say nine as well.

Tests: node tests/run.js cpu-level, node tests/run.js runtime-cache

* docs(std): point the byte-class kernels at runtime-bytes.c and fix the run comment

The runtime table's comment named the wrong C unit for nish/bytes's
byte-class walkers, and JsonTokenizer.string()'s comment on the plain-run
skip described the old per-byte loop. Goldens move by line offset only.

* test(cli): drop str_surrogate_pair from the --emit-ts known list

The case agrees with native under --emit-ts on the head that merges main's
string-row translation (#859), so the corpus check reported it as an unexpected
pass. `node tests/differential/emit-ts.js --update` drops the entry.

Tests: tests/differential/emit-ts-known.txt

* test(cli): keep str_surrogate_pair on the --emit-ts known list

Node 22.23's type stripper rejects an escape the --emit-ts output of this case
spells ("Bad character escape sequence, expected 4 hex characters"), so on CI
the case still differs from native; only an older Node 22 accepts it. The entry
main generated stays, and this reverts the drop.

Tests: tests/differential/emit-ts-known.txt

* test(cli): count all ten runtime units in the --cpu level check

The merge of main brought runtime-term.c in beside runtime-bytes.c and renamed
the check to "all ten runtime units", but its count of `-c runtime*.c` lines
stayed at nine, so the level link with ten compiles failed it.

entries.title: add PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 to nish/crypto/hmac
entries.body: `pbkdf2HmacSha256(password, salt, iterations, length)` derives a key by RFC 8018 §5.2 with HMAC-SHA-256 as the PRF, for the SCRAM-SHA-256 client std/net/postgres will use. The password goes in and the key comes out as a `Secret<u8[]>`: the PRF is keyed once inside `exposeWith` and only the keyed state is copied per round, so no password-derived value is answered plain, and every U_j, T_i, digest and keyed hasher is wiped before return, pinned under opt -O2. Bad arguments answer `null`, like the HKDF Secret forms. Time is linear in `iterations`: a caller taking the count from an untrusted peer must cap it.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: bind a declare function in a package to its bare C symbol
entries.body: A `declare function` in a package other than the program's own (std/ included, which is package `nish`) was emitted under that package's symbol prefix, so `declare function abs` in package `probe` became `@probe.abs` and the link failed. C has one symbol namespace, so a declared function now keeps its name as written in every package. Declarations of one C name that agree on their parameter and return types are one function with one set of facts; declarations that differ are refused (NL3039, naming both). A function the program defines under a declared C name, judged on the symbol it is actually emitted as, is refused at the definition (NL3040), which is newly refused.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: pin use after close of a handle and its sibling shapes
entries.body:
WP40 H1.3. A handle named after its `using` block is a scope error: after
the block, in the loop's next iteration, a `do` loop's condition, a `for`
loop's update, a later `case` (and a `using` written straight into a
clause), the `else`, and a constructor reached by `new`. A lent handle its
callee tries to keep is refused by §4d's rules: a local, a field of another
class, `h.l = this`, and a Map or a Channel at its instantiation. A module
binding is refused first by the module rules. In the handle class's own
constructor, `this` cannot be lent, called, stored or aliased (#566). Shapes
H1.1 already pinned are cited, not duplicated. No shape compiled, so the
compiler is unchanged. LANGUAGE.md states which rule refuses each shape, and
the WP40 status and RT-20's test list record that H1's bar is met.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: give Math.round, min and max JavaScript's -0 and NaN, and add atan2, tan, hypot, sign, imul and f32ToBits
entries.body:
Float `Math.round`, `Math.min` and `Math.max` now answer as JavaScript
does: a NaN operand gives NaN, `min(0, -0)` is -0, and a value in
[-0.5, 0) rounds to -0. That withdraws two documented deviations and
retires NL8010. Native builds lower min and max to the compare-and-select
C compilers emit; wasm keeps `llvm.minimum`/`maximum`.

`Math.atan2`, `Math.tan` and `Math.hypot` are new, written in Nish in
`std/math.ts` as ports of fdlibm and copied into each calling module as
internal functions, so no target calls libm for them and every target,
wasm included, gives the same answer. Every NaN, signed zero and infinity
case is JavaScript's, and ordinary arguments are within one ulp of the
exact value, pinned in CI by sampled mpmath references across every
reduction branch. `Math.sign`, `Math.imul` and the `f32ToBits` builtin are
new too. Under `--emit-ts`, float min, max and round are plain `Math` again
and an i64 `Math.sign` goes through a `bigint` helper.

Measured: atan2 224-229 ms vs Go 274-319 ms; tan 212-218 vs Go 231-235 ms;
hypot 60.3 vs Go 68.5-71.3 ms; all three under C and Rust (min of 21
interleaved runs, band 0.3-2.8% Nish, 1.4-16% Go)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: refuse attacker-facing code that ships without its security record
entries.body:
A std/net or std/crypto module, a runtime C file, or a builtin that reads
the network, the terminal or another process now lands with its
docs/security/ record and index row. CLAUDE.md's definition of done and
ARCHITECTURE.md's construct checklist say so, and scripts/security-scope.mjs,
run by CI and npm test, refuses a file that no record's Scope table or index
row names. The six files that predate the rule are listed under "Not yet
audited" with a reason, and the list only shrinks.

A CodeQL workflow analyses runtime/*.c with its actions pinned to commits;
its first alerts are triaged in docs/security/runtime.md, which also records
the design of a debug arena that would trap a stale reference. SECURITY.md
and std/README.md no longer say nothing in std/crypto is wiped.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: make CI's test shards the full-suite gate
entries.body:
Sessions no longer run the unsharded `npm test` locally before opening a
pull request and again after the last merge of main. Unsharded it takes 40
to 70 minutes in a 4-core cloud session, while CI's `test` job already runs
the whole suite in four cost-dealt shards on every push (about 14 minutes
wall, 46 runner-minutes).

Locally a change now runs `npm run check`, `npm run lint` and
`node tests/run.js <filter>` for every section or program it touches; a
`src/` change still adds the `wasi` and `performance` sections and the
goldens regeneration. The full-suite gate is every CI `test` shard green on
the current head, each shard's summary read for skips and a `DEGRADED:`
banner the way a local run is, with delegated checks named by the job that
proves them. A change to the suite itself, or a fork pull request whose CI
does not run, still runs the whole suite locally and says so in its body.

The rule lives in CLAUDE.md's definition of done; AGENTS.md, the .claude
guides, docs/AI.md, docs/MASTER_PLAN.md and the pending stages of the
active plans point at it.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: nish:term setTerminalRestore writes a mode reset on exit, panic and signal
entries.body:
A full-screen program can now hand the runtime the bytes that undo its escape-sequence modes — alternate screen, hidden cursor, kitty keyboard flags, mouse reporting, bracketed paste — and the runtime writes them to the terminal before it restores termios, on a normal exit, on a panic and on every signal that ends the program (SIGKILL aside). A crash no longer leaves a blank alternate screen with no cursor, or a shell broken by kitty keyboard mode.

setTerminalRestore(bytes) answers 0 when the bytes are kept, -25 when stdout is not a terminal and -7 past 4,096 bytes; a new call replaces them and "" clears them. The bytes go out once, with write(2) only, while every signal is blocked, so a second fatal signal cannot cut them short. Ctrl-Z and setRawMode(false) write nothing. Under Node and in --emit-ts output the builtin throws, as setRawMode does; the WASI runtime answers -25.

This also registers the std modules nish/term-io, term-pixels, term-probe, term-rate and base64 as placeholders, so the stages that fill them touch neither the module list nor the release gates.

entries.title: add nish/cli, and paint --help in the terminal theme's colours
entries.body:
`nish --help` painted its headings, flags and placeholders in fixed 256-colour tones, which ignored the colours the reader's terminal theme sets. It now uses only the eight basic ANSI colours, bold and faint, which every theme redefines, so the help takes on the reader's palette. On a terminal whose TERM terminfo declares no colours (`tput colors` below 8, as for TERM=vt100), headings and flags are bold and placeholders underlined instead. Forced colour (FORCE_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE) is always the theme's and asks nothing, since its reader is a pager or an editor that paints the escapes itself.

The help menu moves into the standard library as `nish/cli`, so a Nish program can print a help that behaves the same way: `HelpMenu` builds it a line at a time with descriptions lined up at the caller's columns, `Style` paints it, and `styleFor(fd, agent)` and `agentDriven()` are the policy the compiler follows. `HelpMenu` and `Style` reach no capability. The compiler imports the module by a relative path, so `std/cli.ts` may use only what the last release compiles.

The colour probe runs tput as /usr/bin/tput or /bin/tput, never through PATH, so a PATH holding `.` cannot run a tput planted in a checkout when someone types `nish --help` there.
tests: tests/link/std_cli; tests/run.js exit-codes ("--help on a monochrome terminal (vt100)"
"--help: the colour probe never runs a `tput` found on PATH")

entries.title: a std/threads task may call a function that wipes memory the task allocated
entries.body:
A `wipe` used to count as a shared write wherever it ran, because its
body is a call to `llvm.memset` and a call with no body is a shared
write. NL2471 therefore refused any std/threads task or parallel body
that zeroed scratch it had allocated itself, so a password hash could not
run on a worker thread.

The wipe's write now moves to the argument it is given, composed like any
other write through a call: an array the function allocated stays
private, and a parameter, a capture, a field, a call's answer or a
`Secret` made with `secret(...)` is still a shared write. The wipe is
still one volatile `llvm.memset`, and `sharedWrite` feeds no LLVM
attribute, so the emitted IR does not change.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: audit regex, term, bytes, PBKDF2 and the browser host
entries.body:
Five attacker-facing areas had no security record. Each is now audited,
its findings fixed with a test or accepted in writing, and its record
indexed in docs/security/README.md.

- nish/regex: compile time and memory are bounded for patterns an
  attacker writes (empty-body repeats, 10,000-range classes, 1,024
  groups, the slot table); iteration's quadratic case is documented.
- nish:term: the screen, cell count and CSI parameters are capped, and
  the terminal is restored on every catchable signal, including one
  that arrives while raw mode is being entered.
- nish/bytes: the N-API shim refuses a typed array longer than 2^31-1,
  and no std/crypto module calls a variable-time scan kernel.
- PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256: recorded under crypto-k1 (K1-8, K1-9).
- Browser adapter: runs with only web globals, with a declaration file.

entries.title: link the speed profile in parallel
entries.body:
The speed profile's link spent most of its time in full LTO's code
generation, which ran on one core. When the link goes through lld, the
speed link now splits that code generation into one partition per core
(-Wl,--lto-partitions=<cores>; cores from nproc, else getconf
_NPROCESSORS_ONLN, else sysctl -n hw.ncpu). The whole program is still
optimised as one module, so inlining is unchanged and the instructions a
program runs stay within a few of bench/instructions.json. macOS ld64 and
the GNU ld fallback have no partition flag and link as before, and the
size, napi, debug, wasm and wasi profiles are unchanged.

ThinLTO linked faster (cold 5.6 s) but failed the instruction-count
gate (sieve +51%, Permute +20%, nbody +12%), so it was not taken.
Compiling the cached runtime to native objects needs a second compile
flag list for the cache, so it was not taken either.

The bytes now depend on the partition count. One machine still links
one input to one output, as scripts/bootstrap.sh's stage comparison
needs, but machines with different core counts can produce slightly
different speed binaries. The runtime cache key fingerprints
scripts/build.sh, so caches built with the old flags are rebuilt.

Measured: speed --link of tests/link/net_relay_f64, one 4-core machine,
5 interleaved rounds: cold median 11.60 s -> 8.53 s (1.36x), warm 11.22 s
-> 8.12 s; link step alone 8.08 -> 4.93 s (min). Noise band from a
byte-identical base re-run 1.2-1.9%. Runtime: node tests/run.js
performance 237/237; bench --instructions all 21 within +0.100% of
bench/instructions.json. Size: npm run size-report byte-identical;
benchmark binaries within 32 B.

entries.title: a deadline for an HTTP/1 head and HPACK decoding into caller storage (H1-1, H2-1)
entries.body: An HTTP/1 slot was closed only when idle, and the idle clock restarts on every byte, so a client trickling its request head held its slot forever. Http1Config.headTimeout (30 s by default) now bounds a whole request head from its first byte to its blank line; on TLS the clock starts on any post-handshake ciphertext, so a record trickled without handing over plaintext is bounded too. expire(now) closes a slot that is idle or past its head deadline. H2-1 was already fixed by #473; H1-3 stays open, with its reason in docs/security/http1.md.

entries.title: vendor SQLite and link it when a program uses it
entries.body:
The SQLite 3.54.1 amalgamation is vendored, unchanged and public domain, in runtime/sqlite/. scripts/build.sh compiles and links it whenever a program's IR declares an `@sqlite3_*` or `@nishsqlite_*` function, so `nish run`, `--link` and a hand-written build line all link it with no extra flag. A program that does not call SQLite keeps its link line, binary and cache key.

`nish run` and `--link` cache the compiled SQLite objects in their own runtime-cache entry. Its key covers every runtime/sqlite/*.c and *.h, runtime/nish.h, the profile, `--cpu`, `--threads`, the compiler and `NISH_SQLITE_CFLAGS`. SQLite is compiled to native code even under the LTO profiles, so a warm link takes milliseconds rather than ten seconds.

The defaults are SQLite's recommended compile-time options, with `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=0`, or `2` (multi-thread mode: one connection per thread) under `--threads`. `NISH_SQLITE_CFLAGS` appends options, and an option naming a default replaces it.

Per profile: wasi links SQLite and runs it, wasm refuses with exit 2, and a napi addon exports none of SQLite's symbols. docs/security/sqlite.md records the trust model, the options and how to update the version.
metrics: speed-profile link of tests/link/sqlite_link, cold 18.1 s / warm 0.175 s; debug, cold 1.47 s / warm 0.14 s; npm tarball +2.65 MB packed

entries.title: nish/term-rate chooses the refresh rate a machine and link sustain
entries.body:
nish/term-rate is a pure refresh controller. A terminal program tells it each frame's size and build cost, and when the terminal acknowledges each frame, through the reply to an in-order query sent after it. It answers whether a frame may be drawn now and at what tier, from 5 to 60 fps (120 on request). It also answers what resolution divisor, backend cap and colour depth to draw at.

- **What it measures.** It keeps three loads under a 70% budget: build cost against the frame time, bytes against the measured throughput, and the round trip against the frames allowed in flight. At most one or two frames are unacknowledged at once, so lag cannot build up on a slow link even when every write returns at once.
- **When it changes rate.** It drops after 1 s over budget, rises after 3 s comfortably under, and settles after each change, so the rate does not oscillate.
- **Starting rate and overrides.** It starts at 15 fps on a remote link and 30 on a local one; a probe round trip outranks stale SSH variables. Overrides are `fixedFps`, `maxFps`, `minFps`, `allow120` and `NISH_TERM_FPS`.
- **When the lowest acceptable rate does not fit.** Under the default, prefer-rate, it cuts the bytes rather than the rate: half and quarter resolution, then half-blocks, then 256 colours, and undoes these as the link recovers. A link whose round trip is all latency instead falls below the floor at full detail, because smaller frames cannot help it.
- **Throughput.** It is measured as bytes acknowledged over the time the link was busy, so a burst of acknowledgements does not read as unbounded bandwidth.
- **Robustness.** An acknowledgement for a frame already given up as lost is swallowed rather than matched to a later frame. Non-finite inputs are ignored.
- **Stats overlay.** drawStatsOverlay prints the current tier, backend, round trip, throughput, frame cost and dropped frames into a corner of a nish/term Screen.

The module reaches no capability and reads no clock.
metrics: 19.3 ns a frame for tick, mayDraw, frameSent and ackReceived together (19.25–19.98 ns over 4×6 warm runs of 2M frames)

a link that degrades and recovers

entries.title: libFuzzer harness, sanitizer runtime build, CI fuzz jobs, JSON/URL/regex targets
entries.body:
The std parsers that read untrusted bytes are now fuzzed with libFuzzer. scripts/fuzz.sh builds any tests/fuzz/targets/<name>.ts under -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined and adds sanitize_address to every compiled Nish function, so ASan covers the Nish code as well as the C runtime and harness. UBSan covers only the C. Under -DNISH_FUZZ_ABORT a panic, a failed check or an out-of-memory aborts, so libFuzzer records it as a crash.

There are five targets with seed corpora: json-tokenizer, json-value, json-typed, url and regex. Each checks the parser against a second way of computing the same answer. tests/run.js gains a fuzz section, which replays the corpora and regressions, and a runtime_sanitize section, which runs the runtime unit test under ASan and UBSan. CI runs a fixed-seed smoke run on every PR, bounded by wall-clock time, and a weekly 30-minute run per target that uploads crash files.

RT-21 is fixed: nish_argv_init tested malloc's result for null only after offsetting it.

entries.title: link most tests/link programs under a cheaper profile
entries.body:
Most tests/link programs now link under --profile debug instead of build.sh's default speed profile (-O3 -flto). The profile changes the link, never the IR, so goldens, expected.ir and the wipe checks read what they read before. SPEED_LINK in tests/run.js names the 43 programs that keep speed, each with its reason: alias metadata in expected.ir, the arr_ aliasing domain, wipes that must survive -O2, SIMD kernels, RSS and timing bounds, and four programs whose debug run costs more than the speed link saves. A program whose args name a profile keeps it. The other sites that link a tests/link program go through the same linkProfile rule, and the startup-byte budgets and the p256 seam pin speed explicitly. A no-compile guard (node tests/run.js speed-link) fails when a listed name has no tests/link program, when a program with !tbaa, noalias or !alias.scope in its expected.ir, or one a wipe check covers, is missing from the list, or when a listed program's args already name a profile. tests/shard-costs.json is re-measured from this change's CI shards.

No program's exit code or stdout differed between the two profiles. The link loop stays sequential: no parallel link loop was on main to measure.

entries.title: translate the array and record rows in --emit-ts
entries.body:
`--emit-ts` now translates the array and record rows. An element read or
store the checker did not prove in range goes through the runtime's
`idx`/`setIdx`, which panic with the native out-of-range message; a
compound element store checks the index again after its right side runs,
as native does, so a right side that shrinks the array panics rather than
growing it back. `new Array<T>(n)` is filled with T's zero (`0`, `0n`,
`false`, or `null` for a nullable T), `pop` of an array not proven
non-empty panics, and `dst.set(src, at)` copies in place.

A record held inline in an array is copied in at a push, a literal or a
store, decided by the slot's type, so a `(P | null)[]` slot still shares
its reference. A generic whose instances would need different copies or
zeros is refused with NL4013. A module that binds a helper's name, such as
its own `idx`, gets the helper imported under a `__nish_` alias in the
records and numbers rows.

entries.title: an elision-off reference build and a soundness differential
entries.body:
An internal --no-elision flag compiles every bounds check, null check and
overflow check the optimiser would otherwise prove away, so a program built
with it is a reference for the same program built with elision. The new
tests/differential/soundness.js builds each generated or listed program both
ways at -O2 and requires that stdout and exit status match and that the
optimised build takes no trap the checked build lacks. A difference is an
elision the compiler should not have made.

tests/run.js pins the no_elision section, and ci.yml runs a fixed-seed pass
of the differential on every pull request. --run-timeout is bounded to what
Node's timer accepts.

entries.title: seed the string hash of every Map and Set (JSON-13)
entries.body:
Map<string, V> and Set<string> now hash strings with SipHash-1-3 under a per-process random 128-bit key, filled from getentropy by a module constructor before main. A program can no longer pick keys that all share one hash and turn every lookup into a linear scan. Insertion order is unchanged.

The instruction gate pins the key for counting only, with a getentropy preload in bench/, so string-map counts stay deterministic; the shipped runtime is unchanged.

entries.title: Framebuffer and the kitty, Sixel, half-block and ASCII backends
entries.body:
A program draws RGB pixels into a nish/term-pixels Framebuffer at a resolution it chooses. Pure encoders then turn it into four outputs:
- **kitty graphics:** standard base64 in 4096-byte chunks, through one reused image id. Each frame is transmitted in place, so the old one stays on screen until the new one has fully arrived. kittyDelete frees the image on close. Direct transfer is the only mode; the module leaves a seam for shared memory and zlib.
- **Sixel:** a fixed 6×7×6 palette, with optional 4×4 ordered dithering. Every register always holds the same colour, so nothing flickers from frame to frame.
- **Half-blocks:** drawn through nish/term's Canvas, which diffs.
- **ASCII:** a luminance ramp, limited to 16 colours on the Linux console.

fitFramebuffer letterboxes the image into the window and keeps its aspect ratio. scaleFramebuffer downscales by an integer divisor, for the refresh controller's resolution step.

The encoders keep their working arrays on the caller's reused PixelBytes. Those arrays grow by doubling to the largest frame, so encoding frame after frame allocates nothing. Over 2000 frames, peak memory stays at 11 MB, where per-call scratch reached 562 MB.

nish/base64 adds the standard RFC 4648 encoder with padding: base64EncodedLength, base64EncodeInto (no allocation) and base64Encode. It is separate from crypto's base64url.

Both modules are pure and give the same bytes under Node.
metrics: per 480×270 frame into 200×60 cells, kitty 0.33 ms, Sixel 10.1 ms (20.7 ms dithered), half-block 0.08 ms, ASCII 0.04 ms (100 frames × 5 runs, noise ≈3%)
tests: a second kitty frame under the reused id

entries.title: mark ECT on QUIC datagrams the carriers send (QUIC-10)
entries.body: Recovery already validated ACK_ECN counts and reacted to CE, but no carrier marked ECT, so on a deployed server every ACK_ECN failed validation and a CE rise was never used. The HTTP/3 server now marks each slot's connection and sends every flight with its codepoint. A flight is cut where marking stops, at the end of the ten testing packets, because one GSO send carries one codepoint. Where the platform refuses a marked send (Darwin, -95), the send goes again unmarked and marking is turned off for every slot. QUIC-10 is closed in docs/security/quic.md.

entries.title: refuse a dependency's unsafe, ffi, net and process.spawn unless the root package grants them
entries.body:
A package loaded from node_modules that reaches one of the four gated capabilities (unsafe, ffi, net, process.spawn) is now refused at compile time with NL2576, unless the root package.json grants it that capability by name under "nish": { "capabilities": { "dependencies": { "<pkg>": [...] } } }. The error points into the dependency and names the package, the capability, the function and the chain of calls that reaches it.

Only the root manifest grants: no CLI flag grants, a dependency's own manifest is not read, and the root's deny still wins. A dependency's name comes from where it was installed, never from its own manifest. A malformed grant is NL3041, and an ungated name in a grant is NL3042.

BREAKING CHANGE: a program whose dependency reaches unsafe, ffi, net or process.spawn no longer builds until the root package.json grants that capability to it; each NL2576 error names the grant to add.

Refs: docs/wp40-dependency-capabilities.md, docs/security/capabilities.md
Tests: tests/link/caps_dep_*

entries.title: a proof-shaped program generator and an AddressSanitizer build
entries.body:
A checked build cannot show a wrong bounds proof: the elided access reads a
neighbour's bytes and carries on. Two tools now make such a proof visible.

tests/differential/proofgen.js generates programs shaped like the accesses
the elision reasons about, in 29 kinds: derived indices, trusted loop bounds,
push and pop, the ranged set/slice/fromBytes operations, aliasing, closures,
arena scopes and nish/threads. Each shape has an in-bounds and a one-past
variant, so a checked build's panic is known in advance. It exports
generate(seed, index) with KINDS, PROOF_MISSES, ASAN_BLIND and
LIBRARY_CHECKED. --self-test builds every kind alone in both variants: each
in-bounds variant must prove one of its own accesses, each one-past variant
must keep its check, and each must panic exactly when one past.

tests/differential/asan.js runs a program under AddressSanitizer. It adds
sanitize_address to every define, rewrites each module's inline
nish_alloc_struct to call the runtime, and links against runtime units built
with -fsanitize=address,undefined -DNISH_ASAN. It classifies a run as asan,
ubsan, panic, signal, timeout, error or clean. --self-test has 17 cases.

Under NISH_ASAN only, runtime/runtime.c gives each block its own malloc chunk,
keeps an array's cap at len + 1, and mirrors a normal build's capacity
growth in a global table, so a data pointer kept across a reallocating push
reads poisoned memory and one kept across a non-reallocating push stays
valid. With the macro off, the runtime is unchanged.

Findings: seed 1 with 200 programs and the catalogue found no unsound
elision and no miscompile. The elision proves 382 of 603 accesses. A sweep
of all tests/cases under ASan reported 0 asan, 0 ubsan and 0 signal.

entries.title: add nish/sqlite, a SQLite client
entries.body:
A program imports `nish/sqlite` to open a database, run `exec`, and prepare a statement once to reuse it: bind, step, reset and read columns, with a `Result` for every failure. Nothing is added to the build line. `nish run` and `--link` link the vendored SQLite 3.54.1 as soon as a program uses the module.

Connections and statements are integer handles into tables on the C side. They carry a generation, so a stale, closed or foreign handle answers SQLITE_MISUSE and never reaches a freed object. A slot whose generation wraps is retired rather than reused. Text and blob columns are read into the caller's `u8[]` with one copy (`columnInto`), and binds take windows into the caller's bytes.

The bind, step, reset and column paths allocate nothing. The tests measure the arena inside every pass of a 1,000-row loop and a 1,000-pass rebind loop.

runtime/sqlite/nish-sqlite.c holds one adapter per SQLite call and nothing else: no SQL, no JSON, no application logic. Each adapter is small enough to inline under LTO.

The module needs the `ffi` capability. Under `--deny ffi` it is refused at the call that reaches C. The tables are per thread under `--threads`.

The record is in docs/security/sqlite.md, with SQL-1 (the generation wrap) fixed and SQL-2 (columnText reading a failed conversion as null under memory pressure) open.

entries.title: run the tests/link programs through a worker pool
entries.body:
The tests/link loop in tests/run.js used to link and run its programs one at a time. It now runs them defaultJobs() at a time through tests/pool.js. Each program's body is an async function that records its checks and WROTE lines. The records are replayed through reportCase in linkTests order, so the output is byte-identical to the serial loop at any width, including under --update-link-goldens.

- **Async spawns.** Every child process in the body is spawned asynchronously, so the event loop never blocks.
- **Widths.** `--jobs N` sets the width, and `--jobs 1` is the serial loop. The per-module llvm-as/opt pool inside each program is capped at floor(defaultJobs() / N), so the two levels together stay within the cores.
- **Serial list.** LINK_SERIAL names the programs that must run alone, after the pool. It is empty: two pooled full runs and one at --jobs 1 report identical PASS/FAIL/SKIP lines.
- **Shared state.** Every piece of shared state is shown safe in comments: per-program build directories, the runtime object cache, counters owned by the replay, and port-0 sockets. net_prefork's close-then-rebind window is named, along with why it stays pooled.
- **Shard costs.** tests/shard-costs.json is regenerated from a CI run of the pooled loop on top of #909's link profile, and docs/wp10-ci.md's shard figures cite that run.

entries.title: nish/term-io opens a terminal and runs a frame loop that adapts to it
entries.body:
`nish/term-io` is the term module that does the I/O. `runTerminal(options,
state, update, render)` opens the terminal, steps `update` at a fixed rate and
calls `render` only when the refresh controller (`nish/term-rate`) lets a frame
go, then closes it. `openTerminal` answers a `Terminal` for a program's own
loop, with `readEvents`, `present`, `stats` and `close`.

Opening refuses a pipe on stdin or stdout with one sentence. It enters raw mode
and the alternate screen and probes the terminal (`nish/term-probe`). Then it
turns on the kitty keyboard, mouse, paste and focus reports the options ask
for. Before each change reaches the terminal, the runtime's restore string is
set to undo everything so far, so a panic or a signal leaves the terminal as it
was.

`present` draws the screen and the framebuffer in one write, with the best
backend the terminal has (kitty graphics, Sixel, half blocks, ASCII) capped by
the controller. A DSR 5 query follows the frame, and its answer acknowledges
the frame to the controller. The send time is taken before the write, so the
round trip covers the frame's whole transmission. A frame's cost is update,
render and encode, without the write.

Every terminal reply stays inside term-io: only frame acknowledgements reach
the controller, and a late probe answer still teaches the cell size. Closing
reads the acknowledgements still in flight before raw mode ends, so none
echoes into the shell over a slow link.

`examples/term-probe.ts` prints what was detected and a stats line a second,
for bug reports. `bench/term-io.mjs` measures `present` per backend. The guide
gains a terminal-programs page, and the standard library reference gains
`nish/base64` and the `nish/term` event API.

The tests run the module in a pseudo-terminal that answers like kitty and
models a link's latency and bandwidth (`tests/term-io/relay.mjs`). They cover:
the guide's program quitting on q and on Ctrl-C; both pipe refusals; the
restore bytes after a panic; throttling on a slow link, including the
bandwidth it measures and at most one unacknowledged frame; acknowledgements
drained on close; late replies kept from the program; the watermark; and
steady-state RSS per forced backend, with a planted leak caught.
`--deny tty` refuses a program that opens the terminal.

Smoke runs read /dev/null, and the soundness runner times a run out by its own
timer rather than racing spawn's SIGTERM.

entries.title: measure nish/sqlite against C on the challenge schema
entries.body:
bench/sqlite runs the twelve-dollar server challenge's point lookup, its 20-post feed, and an insert in WAL mode two ways: through nish/sqlite, and through the same loop written against SQLite's C API. Both use the vendored sqlite3.c with the flags scripts/build.sh uses. `node bench/sqlite/run.mjs --validate` checks that both sides read the same rows and checksums.

The verdict statistic is the median. A difference is claimed only when it exceeds the noise band (the build against its byte-identical copy) and both sides' IQR. Under that rule:
- the feed (21 steps, 100 column reads and a reset per call) costs under 1 µs more than C, 2 to 6 % across three sessions;
- the lookup and both inserts are not measurable.

Nish − C includes the adapter's handle and row checks, which the C loop doesn't make.

The measurement found one adapter fix: `nishsqlite_column_into` asks SQLite for the column count once when a row is current, with every answer unchanged. tests/link/std_sqlite_norow pins the no-row branch. Before the fix the feed was at +1,319 ns, and most of that gap was the benchmark's own fold.

The challenge's schema and queries, and the seed generator ported from its seed/generate.mjs, are MIT and are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

entries.title: a capability lockfile that fails a build when a dependency reaches a new capability
entries.body: `--update-capability-lock` writes `nish-capabilities.lock.json` beside the nearest package.json. The file records the capabilities each dependency reaches. Once the file exists, every build is held to it. A dependency that reaches a capability its row does not record fails the build with NL2577. The message names the dependency, the capability, the function and the call chain. A dependency that reaches less than its row records still builds. The flag writes the file only after the dependency policy has passed. A lockfile that cannot be read is refused with NL3043. `nish run` checks the lockfile before it looks in the run cache, so a cached binary is still held to the current file.

entries.title: nish/term-rate keeps its latency and bandwidth estimates apart on small frames
entries.body:
Over ssh with one frame in flight, 60 ms away at 300 kB/s, a run of 1.5 kB
frames slid the latency to about 4 ms and left the bandwidth to carry the
round trip: it decayed to about 24 kB/s, a twelfth of the link. The latency
crept up by a 256th of each answer's gap while every small trip pulled the
bandwidth toward its own bytes over its whole round trip, so the two traded
off.

They are now measured apart. A frame sent onto an idle link makes a trip,
kept with the last 16 and the probe's. Two trips of different sizes measure
the bandwidth from the difference, which the latency is no part of; a frame
that waited behind the previous answer measures its bytes over the time
since that answer. The latency is the least, over the kept trips, of the
round trip less the trip's bytes at the bandwidth. No sample divides by a
near-zero time, so the first answers no longer read hundreds of MB/s.

Frames of one size with no probe cannot tell latency from bytes, so the
bandwidth stays unknown there and the round-trip load decides alone; detail
is no longer cut for a gain that is not there. Samples stop counting for
decisions 5 s after the last one, so a link that narrows is followed; the
reported figure keeps the last sample until a newer one replaces it or three
trips in a row contradict it. A non-finite probe time, and an answer read no
later than its frame was sent, time nothing. The public API is unchanged.

nish/term-io's throttle check now asserts the bandwidth estimate on the
last, small frames rather than the run's peak.

Moved traces against main: swing falls 60, 15, 10 over a second instead of
straight to 10, because the latency step is no longer read as a narrow link;
widen restores detail 200 ms sooner, because the first quick answer proves
the bandwidth; thin gains a 20 ms probe, without which its equal frames
cannot measure the bandwidth.
metrics: small frames at 60 ms / 300 kB/s, probed: 24.7 kB/s and 4.3 ms before, 270.7 kB/s and 59.5 ms after (deterministic simulation); term-io throttle final estimate on a 300 kB/s link: main 70-86 kB/s (3 runs), this change 218-304 kB/s (9 runs)

The restore string turns modes off in the order they were turned on, and the
docs no longer say it reverses them. The standard-library guide gains a
`nish/term-pixels` section.

entries.title: bcrypt hash and verify in nish/crypto/bcrypt
entries.body:
`nish/crypto/bcrypt` hashes a password with `$2b$` at cost 4 to 31 from a
16-byte salt the caller draws, and verifies `$2a$`, `$2b$` and `$2y$`
hashes, refusing `$2x$`. Each function returns a `Result`, and malformed
input is an `Err`, never a panic.

The password is a `Secret<u8[]>`. The key schedule and the 2^cost rounds
run inside `exposeWith`, and the Blowfish state (P-array and S-boxes, 1042
words), the expanded key and every other buffer holding key material are
wiped before return. Verify rebuilds the whole hash and compares it with
`timingSafeEqual`.

The key follows libxcrypt's `crypt_r` and crypt_blowfish:
- the first 72 bytes up to the first NUL, plus one NUL;
- a longer password truncated rather than refused, so that every stored
  hash still verifies;
- the `$2a$` sign-extension countermeasure.

docs/security/crypto-bcrypt.md has the table of where OpenBSD and Go differ.
None of those differences is reachable from a UTF-8 password.

The module is pure Nish, with no I/O and no C, and builds for wasm32. The
S-box loads in the round function carry no bounds check.
metrics: 52.1 ms (51.9–52.4) CPU per cost-10 hash against libxcrypt crypt_r $2b$ 48.4 ms (47.5–48.6), OpenBSD bcrypt.c gcc -O2 48.4 ms (47.9–48.4) and clang -O2 53.9 ms (53.5–54.1); median of 5 rounds of 8 hashes, min–max band

entries.title: fuzz targets for TLS, QUIC, HPACK, HTTP/1, WebSocket and X.509
entries.body:
Adds libFuzzer targets with seed corpora for the TLS record and handshake parsers, QUIC packet and frame parsing, HPACK, HTTP/1 requests and responses, WebSocket frames, and DER, PEM and X.509. They run on the ASan+UBSan harness from #908. The per-PR fuzz-smoke job now runs every target for 30 s, which keeps the step inside its timeout. The scheduled long run covers the new targets.

The runs found two C runtime findings, RT-20 (Medium) and RT-21 (Low). Both are fixed, regression-tested and recorded in docs/security/. Each area record now names its fuzz targets and their run results, and docs/security/README.md gains a Fuzzed section that maps records to targets.

entries.title: a JSON-plain byte class, and JsonWriter's byte writers on it
entries.body:
nish/bytes gains skipJsonPlain, a fourth byte-class run: every byte a JSON writer copies unescaped, 0x20 to 0xff other than `"` and `\`, with no UTF-8 check. It lowers to a new kernel in runtime/runtime-bytes.c with scalar and 16-byte (SSE2, NEON, wasm SIMD) paths of its own, on its own pointer set by the existing resolver. The three existing classes' loops are instruction-identical to before. The unit is 1,525 of its 1,536-byte budget.

JsonWriter.keyBytes and stringBytes now copy each run of plain bytes in a window of 16 bytes or more with copyBytes, escaping only where the kernel stops. Output is byte for byte unchanged, and a full buffer is still all-or-nothing. The string path that jsonEncode uses is unchanged.

The follow-up also records why S6a's serialize condition is not reached by the escape scan on citm_catalog.json: 95.8% of its strings are under 16 bytes, so the ceiling is 1.0139x, inside serialize's 1.4% band, and a free check would reach only 1.137x. Number writing (37.4% of serialize's instructions) is the next lead. The profile, the guard and the A/B are in docs/wp38-simd.md.

In the A/B against main, two json-compare rows sit just past their bands on unchanged code (tokenize citm 0.994x, typed-reuse 0.955x), recorded as layout noise. bench/json-tokenizer is 0.99x, inside its band.

tests/run.js runs net_relay_soak alone after the link pool (#927): it bounds its resident growth per checkpoint interval, and pooled programs beside it changed that reading. No threshold or check changes.
metrics: JsonDocument.write 1.49x on twitter.json (band 0.4%), 1.03x-1.07x on citm (band 2.7%); serialize on citm 0.988x (band 1.4%)
